Three people at the same Pune start-up got offers in the same month, and each handled the conversation differently.

Farida spent a week on it before speaking to anyone. She looked up what similar roles paid in the city, asked two peers, and listed what she could do that others could not. Then she wrote two numbers on a sticky note: the figure she hoped for, and the lowest she would accept.

Kabir made a different list. He fixed the smallest overall pay-and-perks deal he could live with, along with what else counted for him, such as days working from home and a learning budget. When the recruiter pressed him to answer on the spot, he said, "I'd like to think overnight," and did not feel cornered.

Vinita was so scared the offer would disappear that she said yes before the recruiter had finished the sentence. A month later she learned two colleagues at her level earned more. She thought about how not asking a single question had cost her.

Farida settled a little under her target. That evening she wrote what had worked, and asked her manager Swati for a review date. She began to gather numbers on the projects she delivered, to back a firmer ask in the next round.

qa.q: What two numbers did Farida write on the sticky note?
qa.a: She wrote the figure she hoped for and the lowest she would accept.

qa.q: How did Vinita's answer differ from Kabir's, and what did each cost or protect?
qa.a: Vinita said yes at once from fear and later found colleagues at her level were paid more, while Kabir decided his lowest package beforehand and so could ask for time instead of agreeing under pressure.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she said yes before the recruiter finished?
qa.a: She was afraid the offer would vanish, so she rushed to accept it.

qa.q: What made Farida's review date with Swati a useful step?
qa.a: It gave her a set time and measurable results to back a firmer ask in the next round, even though she settled a little under her target.

grounding: An approach comparison for negotiating a salary: researching ranges, deciding a walk-away point, accepting the first offer from fear, and reviewing the outcome to prepare for the next round.

Thirty days before the board exams, Pallavi sat with her syllabus and gave every topic two ratings: how many marks it usually carried, and how sure she felt about it. The topics with heavy weight and middling confidence went to the top of her list, because an hour spent there would gain the most.

Then she took the exam dates and counted backward, took away rest days and gave each subject its revision blocks. The final pair of days ahead of every paper stayed clear for a light review and sleep, with no new material.

Jasleen took another road. She went back to Chapter 1 of every book and began again from scratch. By the third week she had covered half of each syllabus, and the final chapters, the ones that carried the most marks, were still untouched. She skimmed them the night before, with red eyes.

Nikita, in the middle of the month, laid out her tick-marks and saw she was four chapters behind. She showed her teacher a list of topics that rarely appeared in past papers, and with the teacher's agreement dropped them. The hours she saved went to the areas that showed up in every paper.

qa.q: How many ratings did Pallavi give each topic?
qa.a: She gave each topic two ratings: its usual marks and how sure she felt.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's plan differ from Pallavi's, and what happened to the final chapters?
qa.a: Jasleen started again from Chapter 1 of every book and ran out of time, leaving the heavily weighted final chapters for a hurried skim, while Pallavi ranked topics and counted backward from the exam dates.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when she saw she was four chapters behind?
qa.a: She was probably worried and pressed for time, but she acted by seeking her teacher's agreement to cut topics.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do next time to avoid her problem?
qa.a: She could rate topics by marks and confidence and work backward from the exam dates, so the biggest gains come first.

grounding: An approach comparison for planning last-month exam revision: triaging topics, a backward calendar with buffer days, relearning everything from scratch, and a mid-month check that cuts low-yield topics.

Thomas, Sabina and Charu wanted a site where their school could share notes. At first everybody had wild ideas. Then Charu said, "Version one is a single page with PDFs sorted by subject." Accounts and star ratings could wait.

They split the job in three: Sabina on design, Charu on content, Thomas on coding. They noted the owner and deadline of each task in a shared spreadsheet, and met twice each week for ten minutes, standing in the corridor, to see who was stuck.

Meher, in the next class, was building a study app of her own alone. She added a chat window, achievement stars and a night theme before showing it to anyone. Exams came, her free weeks ran out and nothing went live, while her classmates were after nothing more than a plain timetable.

The notes page went up in three weeks. Sabina checked the visit counts and saw that nobody opened the third page, the one with past-year question papers. She asked around. "I couldn't find it," a boy said. She moved the link to the homepage, waited a week and looked again. The visits to that page had climbed.

qa.q: How often did Thomas, Sabina and Charu meet, and for how long?
qa.a: They met twice a week for ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Meher's approach differ from the trio's, and what happened to each project?
qa.a: Meher added a chat window, stars and a night theme before anyone used it and launched nothing, while the trio started with a simple page and split the work, so their notes page went up in three weeks.

qa.q: What was Sabina thinking when she saw nobody opened the third page?
qa.a: She wondered why, and sought a reason instead of assuming people were not interested.

qa.q: What could Meher do now to get her project out?
qa.a: She could put out a basic timetable page for classmates and add the extra features later based on what they use.

grounding: An approach comparison for building a small online project: defining a minimum first version, dividing roles, overbuilding features before anyone uses it, and iterating from feedback and visit counts.

For two months Sangeeta and Jomon wrote down every rupee in a shared app. They were surprised: food delivery and subscriptions were eating about a fifth of what came in. It reshaped their plan.

They also owed money on a credit card and had an education loan with lower interest. They decided to clear the card first and keep making the minimum payment on the loan, and saw that the order counted for more than small extras spread everywhere.

Her friend Irawati did it differently. She and her husband made a strict budget with no fun money at all. It held for six weeks, then one birthday dinner broke it. They felt they had failed, and threw the whole plan away.

When Sangeeta's salary went up in the autumn, she and Jomon did not just raise spending. They split the extra into three parts: bigger savings, one modest treat for themselves and a fund for her parents. They rewrote the plan that night and pinned it to the fridge.

"If you're unsure about debts, ask someone qualified," Jomon told Irawati over tea. She nodded and picked up her notebook.

qa.q: How long did Sangeeta and Jomon write down their spending?
qa.a: They wrote down every rupee for two months.

qa.q: How did Irawati's strict budget differ from the couple's revised plan, and what did each teach?
qa.a: Irawati's plan had no fun money and collapsed after one dinner, so they abandoned it, while Sangeeta and Jomon rewrote their plan with room for a small upgrade, showing rigid rules can undermine consistency.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after the birthday dinner broke the budget?
qa.a: She felt she had failed, and gave up the plan out of disappointment.

qa.q: Who could help Irawati with questions about her debts?
qa.a: Someone qualified, such as a financial adviser, as Jomon suggested.

grounding: An approach comparison for managing a household budget: tracking expenses, prioritising debts, a strict budget that collapses, and revising categories after an income change.

On a Sunday, Tejas arrived on the terrace with a sheet of paper. "Twenty rules," he said proudly, and began to read. By rule six Dilnaz was looking at the water tank. By rule eleven, half the children were arguing about a different game. Nobody remembered rule three and everyone drifted downstairs to play something else.

The next Sunday, Dilnaz said, "Let's make it out of games we already know." They took the chasing from tag and the safe line from kabaddi, and had a working game in ten minutes instead of inventing it all fresh.

They played a quick five-minute round with the details still loose. The same fast runner won every time. "Not fair," muttered Tejas, who was that runner and knew it. So they added a rule: runners must hop over the final stretch.

Then Chandrika, Dilnaz's six-year-old cousin, got caught first, again, and her face crumpled. The bigger children looked at one another. Dilnaz drew a chalk circle in the corner. "Little ones can't be caught in here," she said. Chandrika wiped her nose, stepped inside, and the game started up again with everyone in it.

qa.q: How many rules did Tejas bring to the terrace?
qa.a: He brought twenty rules.

qa.q: How did Tejas's twenty rules differ from the trial round the following week, and what happened to the players' interest?
qa.a: The twenty rules lost the children before play began and they wandered off, while borrowing from known games and testing a five-minute round gave them a working game and exposed the runner problem to fix.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she was caught first again?
qa.a: She was upset and discouraged, with her face crumpling, at being out first again.

qa.q: What did the chalk circle change for the youngest player?
qa.a: It gave little ones a safe place where they could not be caught, so Chandrika stayed in the game.

grounding: An approach comparison for planning a game with rules: copying rules from known games, a quick trial round, making many rules first, and adapting the game for the youngest player.

When the market fell sharply, Keerthana did not open the app every hour. She asked herself when she would need the money. Some of it was for retirement, decades away. The rest was for a flat deposit in two years. The two pots deserved different thinking.

Simran, her colleague, kept a written plan from a calm afternoon. When the mix drifted, it told her to shift a little money out of the steady holdings and into shares. Keerthana copied the idea onto a page of her own, and followed it when the fear came, not her mood.

Pradeep watched the losses daily and read alarming posts each night. His stomach hurt. One evening he sold everything to make it stop. Months later the market recovered without him, and the loss he had feared became one he had fixed in place.

Keerthana dug out notes from a milder dip two years back, which had recovered. She read how she had felt then. She stayed with her plan but reduced her share in one risky sector.

"For anything big, talk to a qualified adviser," she told Pradeep over lunch. He rubbed his eyes and said he would think about it.

qa.q: What did Keerthana ask herself when the market fell?
qa.a: She asked when she would need the money.

qa.q: How did Pradeep's choice differ from Simran's written rule, and what happened after the recovery?
qa.a: Pradeep sold everything to stop the pain, so when the market recovered without him his loss became permanent, while Simran followed a rule written in a calm period instead of acting on emotion.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he sold everything one evening?
qa.a: He was anxious and in pain from the daily losses and the fearful posts, and wanted the feeling to stop.

qa.q: What did Keerthana's notes from the earlier fall add to her plan?
qa.a: They reminded her that a smaller fall had recovered, so she kept her plan while lowering her exposure to one risky sector.

grounding: An approach comparison for responding to a market crash: reviewing goals and time horizon, rebalancing by written rule, panic selling at the bottom, and learning from a past fall.
